uncited: It sets itself apart from standard splatting by using a multi-resolution pyramid structure to adapt the rendering resolution to the desired image quality, and from [Multi-Resolution Points](4784-multi-resolution-points.md) by explicitly constructing a hierarchical pyramid of averaged volume cells rather than just selecting points based on density or distance.
**Inputs:** A 3D volume dataset of size $N^3$ samples, a viewing direction, and a user-supplied precision threshold (or desired image quality level).
**Pyramid Data Structure:** A sequence of $\log_2(N)$ volumes.
*   Level 0: The original dataset of size $N^3$.
Created by averaging each $2 \times 2 \times 2$ group of samples from level $k-1$.
**Octtree:** Constructed by fitting an octtree to the pyramid based on the user-supplied precision threshold.
**Build Pyramid:** Construct the pyramidal volume representation.
For an original dataset of $N^3$ samples, create $\log_2(N)$ volumes.
**Fit Octtree (Optional/Implicit):** Fit an octtree to the pyramid using the user-supplied precision threshold.
**Determine Resolution Level:** Select the appropriate level of the pyramid to scan based on the desired image quality.
*   Project the volume cell onto the image plane.
*   Approximate the splat with an RGBA Gouraud-shaded polygon.
*   **Binary Data:** For binary data, bits can be packed into bytes (each byte represents a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ portion).
A byte represents an object element if it contains more than four non-zero bits, otherwise background.
*   **Time Complexity:** Building the pyramid takes $O(N^3)$ time.
Rendering time depends on the selected level and the number of cells.
It was designed to enable real-time volume rendering on modern graphics workstations by leveraging hardware-accelerated polygon rasterization.
